newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Philippines gears up for APEC "war".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Philippines gears up for APEC "war".

text.p: For the 27,000 Philippine troops assigned to guard the heads of state attending this month's APEC summit, the task is simple and clear-cut: Prepare for war.
In blazing heat or in the grip of storms, battalions of soldiers and police are holding daily rehearsals to keep U.S. President Bill Clinton and other leaders out of harm's way.
They are preparing for threats from sniper fire and car-bomb attacks to kidnappings and even earthquakes.
"The mindset of a soldier is precision...We always prepare for war," organising committee director general and former Philippine armed forces chief Lisandro Abadia told Reuters.

Abadia assumes all possible threat scenarios even if, as he says, there are no intelligence reports of specific plots against any of the 18 leaders attending the November 25 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit at Subic Bay free port.
"The name of the game here is to embarrass the government ...We should be prepared for the worst," he said.

Abadia spoke to Reuters while his men, braving the rains as a storm lashed Manila one recent weekend, staged mock rescue operations after a simulated terrorist attack on a convention hall where APEC ministers were to meet before the summit.
Near the Manila Hotel, where Clinton and Indonesian President Suharto will stay, riot police came charging in to quell an imaginary protest by leftist protesters.

Concern over security has spurred unpopular measures, including a ban on the entry of Nobel Peace laureate and East Timorese independence leader Jose Ramos Horta and the arrest of Filipino leftist leader Filemon Lagman.
Military intelligence reports accuse Lagman's group of fomenting labour unrest in the hotel, transport and telecommunications sectors to coincide with the APEC meetings.
Stringent security measures have also affected foreign media, with strict visa restrictions on visiting journalists, even if they have been accredited by the APEC organisers.

No satellite broadcasting equipment will be allowed anywhere near the hall in Subic Bay where the leaders will meet and the restrictions effectively mean that nearly all TV coverage from the meeting hall itself will be directly under state control.
One APEC diplomat, a veteran of international meetings, said his own security advisers felt the media curbs were unjustified.
"Is this the face the Philippines wants to present at what is billed as its 'coming-out party'?" the Philippine Daily Inquirer newspaper asked in an editorial.

Organisers said the security measures were justified, given plans by leftist groups to hold a 3,000-car "protest caravan" to Subic Bay on the day of the summit itself and to provoke clashes with police for media mileage.
About 7,000 troops have been deployed around Morong to prevent a threatened incursion into Subic Bay by other leftists with a flotilla of fishing boats, military sources said.
"We have taken every possible scenario into account," a colonel involved in preparations said. "Ambush, kidnapping, sniper fire, bombings, even earthquakes.
"In case of a really big one (earthquake), our men already know what to do and where to bring the delegates to safety," he said.

An average of five to seven shocks, almost all of them imperceptible, strike this earthquake-prone nation daily. Subic is also just a few kilometres from Mount Pinatubo, which erupted in 1991 in the world's biggest volcanic explosion this century.
Philippine armed forces chief General Arturo Enrile said the military was also exchanging information with the United States and other countries on potential extremist threats.
"Definitely security is a major concern because any single incident will tarnish the image of the Philippines," foreign undersecretary Federico Macaranas said.
Despite all the preparations, there is no absolute 100 percent guarantee nothing will go amiss, Abadia said, adding:
"Remember Atlanta?"
